episode_thesis: Katie Kaminski reviews 2024 through CTA style factors: slow trend systems and large markets won while fast systems lost (especially in whipsawed fixed income), so the 'speed' tilt explains most manager dispersion and the right speed depends on whether the next year brings macro change or stress. Discussing a Quantica paper on volatility sizing, both speakers conclude the static-versus-dynamic sizing debate is a philosophy and implementation spectrum (higher Sharpe versus higher return, concentration in outliers versus smoother risk), and on portable alpha they agree that trend plus equities is natural but carries equity-correlation risk and classification and complexity problems.

speakers.name: Katie Kaminski
speakers.role: Guest; managed futures researcher and author (CTA style factors, managed futures ETF paper)
speakers.speaker_note: Employer not named in the transcript. Ledger corrections applied: C02-2 refers to December 2024 and C15-1 is hers.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend-following returns are idiosyncratic each year because they depend on which trends occur; CTA style factors (speed, size, co-movement, correlation) isolate design tilts to explain dispersion.
worldview_premises.support: Factor construction by perturbing one design decision of a plain trend system versus a benchmark; regression of manager returns on the speed factor

worldview_premises.premise: Trend likes macro change and stress; without them it consolidates, and the turn cannot be timed.
worldview_premises.support: Experience of trend cycles; 2024 lacked macro change

worldview_premises.premise: Reactivity (fast signals) pays in recessions or events, slow signals pay in other years, so speed should be balanced over time.
Trend followers are not explicitly long volatility but have a residual long-vol exposure because volatility expands in trends; static sizing gives more of it than dynamic sizing.
worldview_premises.support: Her own CME paper on managed futures and volatility; about 20% correlation to long vol, estimated 40%+ for static sizing (a guess)

worldview_premises.premise: Trend is a behavioural, positively skewed strategy: few markets trend and not often, but when they do the strategy captures most of the move (cocoa 2024).
worldview_premises.support: Investor explanation experience; Quantica hit-rate data

worldview_premises.premise: Trend positions aggregate into a macro-themed exposure built from price moves only; investors use trend to get macro exposure without macro calls.

Portable alpha 'alpha' is relative to the risks removed; managed futures can be long equities, so stacking has correlation risk, but futures give capital-efficient leverage without borrowing cost and trend plus equities is a natural complement.
Hybrid products create classification, benchmarking and complexity problems for investors, solved for example by dedicated risk-mitigation buckets.
A small-universe trend programme is tilted to large markets and is effectively a different strategy.
Managed futures ETFs follow a product life cycle (proliferation, innovation and consolidation, maturation), helped by US regulation changes for active ETFs.
worldview_premises.support: Her paper on the managed futures ecosystem

decision_process.practice: Build CTA style factors by perturbing one design decision at a time against a benchmark trend system and regress manager returns on them.
decision_process.why: Understand return dispersion and which tilts work when

decision_process.practice: Position between static and dynamic volatility sizing depending on volatility window and objective; mix may suit investors.
decision_process.why: Risk mitigation versus risk-adjusted return trade-off

decision_process.practice: Pair replication with bottom-up implementation and risk management.
When blending trend with equities, size trend dynamically, cap equity beta in the trend book, or accept independence.
Large-market tilt in a small universe (about 20 markets); she treats it as a different strategy.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility rises in profitable trends and again at reversals (cocoa 20 to 120%), which both attracts concentration and justifies volatility sizing.
Volatility scaling and static sizing reflect two philosophies: statistical portfolio management versus classic trend following capturing outliers; discretionary macro concentrates on conviction.
Large early-year gains given back annoy investors, making smoothing a behavioural issue.
Trend does best when markets are highly correlated and one macro factor dominates (GFC, 2022), but a volatility-sized book can still be concentrated on that factor.

worldview_premises.premise: Portable alpha today differs from the pre-crisis version because the alpha source (managed futures) is diversifying; it resurged because alternatives are hard to sell when the S&P returns 25% a year.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 2024 speed result is from one year and one factor construction; she says dispersion was not exceptionally large and it is unclear whether it is more than historically.
The 20% and 40% correlation figures with long volatility are 'ballpark' and a guess respectively, with no stated method.

Volatility rise in winning trades is endogenous (higher volatility is part of being a profitable trend), so only the 1.2 versus 1.05 gap is informative; the Quantica sample (1994-2024) has few outliers.
Correlation factor for commodities was positive but cocoa's contribution depends on each manager's exposure; size factor result was mixed.
Ledger corrections: C02-2 was December not November 2024; C15-1 attributed to Katie.
Pension 'risk mitigation bucket' and 'inflation volatility' views are asserted without data.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Kaminski: volatility of inflation, US deficit and policy, the relative pace of central bank cuts (US lagging), the dollar trade, and macro stress or change as the condition for trend; horizon is calendar 2025. Dunne: equity sentiment extremes, tariff and inflation developments, Fed-ECB divergence. Both say turning points cannot be timed.
reader_inferences: (reader) The speed factor's 2024 result is a one-year realisation; both speakers imply speed should be balanced rather than chosen on last year's winner.
(reader) The positive correlation factor in commodities and cocoa's role show that a single market (cocoa) can dominate dispersion, undercutting a purely systematic reading of factors.
(reader) The residual long-volatility claim depends on sizing choice, so the diversification value of trend is not independent of the volatility-targeting rule.
(reader) Neither speaker supplies a statistical test linking trend speed to macro regimes, so the 'reactivity pays in recession' view is theory plus history.

added_claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
added_claims.claim: Trend following is fundamentally a behavioural strategy whose payoff comes from rare, strongly trending markets rather than a high hit rate.
